Mosaic Authorship
moh-ZAY-ik AW-ther-ship
noun phrase (the authorship of the Pentateuch)
From “Mosaic” (of Moses) and “authorship”; the doctrine that Moses, under divine inspiration, is the author of the Pentateuch, the first five books of Scripture.

📖 Biblical Definition

Mosaic authorship is the doctrine, held by the dictionary as the historic faith of the church and the testimony of Scripture itself, that Moses, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, is the author of the Pentateuch—Genesis through Deuteronomy, the books called “the law of Moses.” The Scriptures attest it within themselves: “Moses wrote all the words of the LORD”; and when Moses had made an end of writing the words of this law in a book, he commanded its keeping beside the ark. The Lord Jesus confirmed it, speaking of “the book of Moses” and asking, “Did not Moses give you the law?”; He grounded an argument for the resurrection on what God said to Moses in the bush, and declared that Moses wrote of Him. The apostles likewise ascribe the law to Moses throughout. The dictionary acknowledges that the death of Moses (Deuteronomy 34) and a few editorial notes were added by a later inspired hand, as the church has long recognized, without overturning the substantial Mosaic authorship of the whole. Against this stands the documentary hypothesis (the JEDP theory of Wellhausen and his successors), which fragments the Pentateuch into supposed sources—Yahwist, Elohist, Deuteronomist, Priestly—woven together by post-exilic redactors centuries after Moses, denying his authorship altogether. The dictionary rejects the documentary hypothesis as a critical construction resting on naturalistic assumptions, contradicting the witness of Christ and the Scriptures, and dissolving the historical foundation of the faith. To deny that Moses wrote the law is, in the end, to call the Lord Jesus mistaken; the dictionary holds with Him that Moses wrote, and that he wrote of Christ.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The doctrine that Moses, under inspiration, authored the Pentateuch, attested by Scripture and confirmed by Christ (John 7:19; Mark 12:26); against the documentary hypothesis (JEDP), which fragments the law into late sources and denies Mosaic authorship.

MOSAIC AUTHORSHIP, noun phrase. The doctrine that Moses, under inspiration, authored the Pentateuch.

“Moses wrote all the words of the LORD” (Exodus 24:4).

Confirmed by Christ, who spoke of “the book of Moses” and said Moses gave the law (Mark 12:26; John 7:19).

A few editorial notes (as Moses' death, Deuteronomy 34) were added by a later inspired hand.

Against the documentary hypothesis (JEDP), which denies Mosaic authorship on naturalistic grounds.

📖 Key Scripture

Ex 24:4 — "And Moses wrote all the words of the LORD, and rose up early in the morning, and builded an altar under the hill, and twelve pillars, according to the twelve tribes of Israel."

De 31:24 — "And it came to pass, when Moses had made an end of writing the words of this law in a book, until they were finished,"

Mr 12:26 — "And as touching the dead, that they rise: have ye not read in the book of Moses, how in the bush God spake unto him, saying, I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob?"

Joh 7:19 — "Did not Moses give you the law, and yet none of you keepeth the law? Why go ye about to kill me?"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The documentary hypothesis (JEDP) fragments the Pentateuch into late, competing sources stitched together by post-exilic redactors, denying Mosaic authorship and contradicting the testimony of Christ.

expand to see more

The documentary hypothesis, given its classic form by Julius Wellhausen, divides the Pentateuch among four supposed sources—the Yahwist (J), Elohist (E), Deuteronomist (D), and Priestly (P)—composed over centuries and combined by redactors long after Moses, often centuries after the exile. The dictionary names this a corruption of the doctrine of Scripture. It rests on naturalistic premises that exclude prophecy and inspiration, treats divine names and stylistic variety as marks of separate authors rather than the richness of one, and reconstructs Israel's religion on an evolutionary scheme foreign to the text. Above all, it contradicts the Lord Jesus, who repeatedly ascribed the law to Moses and said Moses wrote of Him.

The dictionary affirms substantial Mosaic authorship while acknowledging, as the church always has, that a later inspired hand recorded Moses' death and inserted a few explanatory notes—an editorial reality wholly different from the wholesale dismemberment the critics propose. To grant a few post-Mosaic glosses is not to concede the documentary hypothesis but to read the text honestly. The stakes are not academic: the historicity of the law, the integrity of the canon, and the trustworthiness of Christ's own testimony stand together. The dictionary holds that Moses wrote the law of God, and that the One greater than Moses confirmed it.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From “Mosaic” (pertaining to Moses, Hebrew Mosheh) and “authorship”; the phrase “the book of Moses” (Greek biblos Mouseos) names the Pentateuch by its author.

expand to see more

Mosheh, Hebrew, Moses, “drawn out” of the water, the lawgiver and prophet.

“The law of Moses” (Hebrew torat Mosheh) names the Pentateuch by its author.

“The book of Moses” (Greek biblos Mouseos) is the Lord's own phrase (Mark 12:26).

JEDP, the four hypothetical sources of the documentary theory, rejected by the dictionary.

“Wellhausen,” the nineteenth-century critic whose scheme gave the hypothesis its classic shape.

Usage

"The teacher defended Mosaic authorship from the testimony of Christ, who said Moses wrote of Him."

"He showed that divine names and varied style mark the richness of one author, not the seams of four."

"She granted the note of Moses' death as a later inspired addition, without conceding the JEDP scheme."
